prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

On the day I set out on the climb, grief saddled in my back like a bag of marbles, my breath like clouds hanging on the low peaks of a mountain, on the day I set out leaving nothing behind, nothing on the bed, no version of myself, just my voice through the night, the voice I use to ward off nightmares. (My voice is a still life in itself, a shroud green and ultramarine deep blue, a bowl of apples and tangerines on a table.) On the day I set out, the mountain is high in front of me, the unreliable god of mist and fog. I have no voice to say how high my fingers must lift as if on a lover's upper lip, to take in the breath of how high my mountain is—white teeth behind a snow cap, numberless springs, cold like the enzymes in spit— a version of me is still asleep: the moving of a limb in sleep. Everything becomes lucid.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker begins a climb burdened by grief, described physically as a weight carried like a bag of marbles on their back.
- Setting out means leaving everything behind, including any former version of themselves, taking only their voice as protection through the night.
- The speaker's voice is compared to a still life painting, rich with color and imagery of ordinary objects like fruit on a table.
- The mountain ahead is portrayed as vast and god-like, ruled by mist and fog, making its true height impossible to express in words.
- A version of the speaker remains asleep even as they climb, suggesting a duality between dreaming and waking selves, until everything becomes clear.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

This poem depicts a solitary, grief-laden journey up a mountain, using vivid sensory and painterly imagery—breath like clouds, a still-life voice of colors and fruit—to convey the speaker's internal state as they leave behind all versions of themselves except their voice. The climb becomes a meditation on the body's duality (waking self versus sleeping self) and culminates in a moment of clarity, suggesting that confronting an overwhelming, god-like natural force can dissolve the boundary between grief and lucid understanding.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Everything

outputs.L1: On the day I set out on the climb, grief saddled my back like a bag of marbles, my breath hanging like clouds on the low peaks of a mountain. On the day I set out, I left nothing behind—nothing on the bed, no version of myself, only my voice moving through the night, the voice I use to ward off nightmares. (My voice is a still life unto itself: a shroud of deep green and ultramarine, a bowl of apples and tangerines resting on a table.) On the day I set out, the mountain rose before me, high and unreliable, a god of mist and fog. I had no voice to say how high my fingers must lift—as if tracing a lover's upper lip—to draw in the breath of how tall my mountain stood: white teeth behind a cap of snow, countless springs running cold as the enzymes in spit. Somewhere, a version of me still slept, a limb shifting in dream. And everything became lucid.
outputs.L2:
On the morning I began my ascent, sorrow rested against my spine like a sack full of marbles, and my exhales drifted like clouds settling over the mountain's lower ridges. That morning, I departed without a trace—nothing remained in the bed, no echo of who I was, only my voice persisting through the darkness, the same voice that keeps nightmares at bay. (This voice exists as its own still life: a burial cloth in shades of emerald and deep ultramarine, alongside a bowl holding apples and tangerines upon a table.)

As I began my journey, the mountain loomed above me, that fickle deity woven from mist and haze. Words failed me when trying to express how far my fingers needed to reach—as though grazing a lover's upper lip—to fully grasp the scale of this peak: white teeth concealed beneath a cap of snow, countless hidden springs, chilled like the enzymes found in saliva. Meanwhile, another version of myself remained in slumber, a limb shifting slightly in rest. And then, suddenly, clarity took hold of everything.
outputs.L3:
# The Climb

I begin the ascent with grief strapped to my back like a bag of marbles—hard, countless, and clicking against each other with every step I take. Each marble holds its own small weight, insignificant alone, but together they pull at my shoulders, a burden I did not choose but must carry nonetheless. The path rises before me, indifferent to what I bring.

To set out is to leave everything behind. I abandon the rooms I have furnished with old habits, the mirrors that once reflected who I used to be. Every former version of myself stays below, folded into the valley like discarded clothing. I take nothing with me except my voice—my only companion, my only armor against the coming dark. It is all I have to face the night with, this fragile instrument of sound, and I wonder if it will be enough.

My voice, when I use it, unfolds like a still life painting—rich with color, layered with the quiet dignity of ordinary things. It carries the image of fruit resting on a table: the deep purple of grapes, the gold of a pear catching light, the soft shadow beneath a bowl. There is nothing dramatic in this comparison, and yet everything is contained within it—stillness, permanence, the quiet insistence that beauty persists even in simple, unmoving forms. This is what I carry forward into the dark: not a shout, but a painting made of breath.

Ahead, the mountain looms—vast, unknowable, something closer to a god than a landform. It wears mist like a robe, fog curling around its shoulders in a way that conceals as much as it reveals. I cannot say how tall it truly is; language fails at the threshold of such scale. Numbers mean nothing here. The mountain simply *is*, ancient and indifferent, ruled by weather patterns older than memory, and I am small against it, marbles and all.

And yet, strangely, part of me has not left the valley at all. A version of myself remains asleep somewhere below, dreaming through all of this—the climb, the grief, the mountain's impossible height. I move forward while that other self stays still, caught in the suspended logic of dreams. There is a duality here I cannot quite reconcile: the waking body ascending, the dreaming mind unaware, both somehow *me*, both somehow necessary. I climb not knowing which self is more real, only trusting that eventually—at the summit, perhaps, or in some quiet moment between fog and clarity—the two will meet, and everything will finally make sense.
outputs.L4:
**Ascent**

I left the house before the birds remembered
how to speak, before the frost had finished
writing its long confession on the grass.
The mountain stood the way grief stands—
enormous, patient, indifferent to the small
weather of a single body climbing.

My breath came out in clouds, and I watched them
rise ahead of me like versions of myself
sent forward to scout the thinning air,
each one dissolving before I could catch up,
each one a ghost of what I'd been
an hour, a year, a decade back.

By the second mile I had shed the self
that laughed too loud at dinner parties.
By the third, the one who lied to doctors
about how much it hurt. The path took them
the way paths take small stones—
without apology, without record.

Somewhere near the tree line I noticed
my voice had become a still life:
a bowl of unnamed fruit, a cluster
of colors that had no hunger left in them,
umber and plum and the pale gold
of something too ripe to be eaten,
too fixed to rot. It sat inside my throat
like a painting nobody had signed,
and when I spoke to no one—
to the wind, to the lichened rock,
to the god I didn't believe in
until the incline made me a believer—
that voice was the only self
I recognized as mine.

I thought of the body that sleeps,
how it walks these same paths
in a country without gravity,
how it forgets teeth, forgets debt,
forgets the exact shape of the face
it lost last spring. And I thought
of the body that wakes, that must
carry water and weight and the specific
ache behind the left knee,
that must remember everything
the sleeping one is allowed to drop.

I climbed until those two bodies
were only a rumor of each other,
until the wind stopped being wind
and became instead a kind of attention,
vast and unhurried, the way a mountain
watches without watching, the way
something old enough to be a god
simply persists, and in persisting,
asks nothing of you but your smallness.

At the top there was no vista
worth a postcard—only cloud,
only the gray erasure of everything
I had meant to see. But standing there,
lungs scraped raw, voice reduced
to its bowl of quiet fruit,
I felt the grief go transparent,
the way a held breath goes transparent
just before you let it go—

not gone, but seen through,
not resolved, but suddenly
the same substance as understanding,
so that for one white, weightless moment
I could not tell the difference
between what I had lost
and what, at last, I knew.
outputs.L5:
# On Everything

Everything is a peculiar word. It claims totality while remaining stubbornly vague—a placeholder for whatever we can't or won't specify. Say "I need to tell you everything" and you promise an impossible completeness, one that language itself can't deliver.

There's a mathematical flavor to the concept. Set theorists have long grappled with the idea of a "set of all sets," only to find it collapses into paradox—Russell's famous problem where the totality of things undoes itself upon inspection. Everything, taken literally, may not be a coherent object at all, but rather a direction we point toward, never quite arriving.

Physicists chase their own version: a theory of everything, unifying gravity with quantum mechanics, the impossibly large with the impossibly small. It's less a specific answer than a hope—that beneath the mess of forces and particles lies a single elegant explanation, and that human minds, evolved to track predators and forage fruit, might somehow grasp it.

Philosophically, everything gestures at questions we can't quite hold steady. Why is there something rather than nothing? What would it mean for a mind to comprehend the totality of existence? These questions don't resolve so much as they reveal the limits of the asking.

And yet in ordinary life, "everything" does humbler work. Everything is fine. That's everything for today. It becomes a soft container for whatever remains unlisted, a way of waving at complexity without cataloging it. In this everyday sense, everything isn't really about totality—it's about trust, an agreement not to demand more detail than the moment requires.

Perhaps that's the real nature of the word: not a description of the world's sum, but a gesture of surrender before it. To say everything is to admit that enumeration has failed, that language has reached its edge, and that some silence or shrug must finish the sentence reality started.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem about setting out on a mountain climb while carrying grief, using rich still-life imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ascent With a Still Life

I pack the mountain into my rucksack
like a bowl of wax fruit—
the grief sits ripest on top,
a plum going soft at the edges,
bruised where I keep touching it
to check it's still there.

The trailhead offers its arrangement:
three white stones,
a dead moth arranged like a comma,
my father's voice folded into a handkerchief
I don't remember packing.

Somewhere below the scree line
a table is set for one who isn't coming.
The cloth is fog. The silverware is birdsong.
I sit down anyway, mid-stride,
uphill, in my body,
and eat the thin air
like bread that keeps un-baking itself.

The mountain does not move
but it rearranges me—
decants me from one silence into another,
the way light decants itself
through a glass of standing water
left too long on a windowsill,
gone the color of old grief,
gone the color of *almost amber*.

I carry the dead the way a still life
carries its instant forever—
peaches that will not rot,
a knife that will not fall,
my mother's hands
frozen mid-gesture
reaching for a mountain
that was never there
until I made it,
stone by stone,
out of the fruit
she left me
to carry up.

At twelve thousand feet
the wax plum finally splits.
Something old and sweet
runs down into the snow,
staining it the color
of a sunset no one painted
because they were all
too busy climbing.

I keep going.
The summit is not an ending.
It's a table cleared
of everything
but light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that blends the physical act of mountain climbing with emotional loss, incorporating a metaphor comparing the speaker's voice to a painted still life.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ascent

The rope bites into my palms like memory—
raw, insistent, refusing to let go.
Each foothold is a negotiation
with gravity and grief, with the mountain's
indifferent shoulder turned against the sky.

I climb because you cannot.
Because somewhere between the third pitch
and the ridge line, I forget
to translate absence into breath,
forget the shape your name makes
in a mouth grown unfamiliar with speaking it.

My voice, when it comes, is a still life—
fruit arranged too carefully in dying light,
oranges gone soft with sweetness,
a wine glass catching the last of the sun
before the painter's hand has to choose
between beauty and truth.
It sits static on canvas, admired,
untouchable. I open my mouth to call out
and what emerges is composition, not song—
something staged, something that knows
it is already memorial.

The switchbacks teach me what sorrow already knew:
that ascent is rarely a straight line,
that you can move upward for hours
and still feel the pull of what's below,
still feel the specific weight
of a hand that isn't there
to steady you at the narrow places.

At altitude, the air thins to something
like the space after a phone call ends—
that particular silence, algebraic,
subtracting a voice from a room.
I breathe it anyway. I breathe it
because the body doesn't know
how to stop wanting oxygen
just because the heart
has filed its own report of insufficiency.

Near the summit, the wind undoes
whatever arrangement I was keeping—
scatters the careful stillness of my grief
like fruit knocked from a table,
like the whole quiet painting
finally admitting it was always
about the leaving light,
not the objects it illuminated.

I reach the top and there is nothing
to plant a flag in but sky.
I say your name into that emptiness
and for once it isn't still life—
it moves, it echoes, it becomes
weather system, becomes
something the mountain
will remember longer than I can,
long after my hands have healed,
long after I've descended
into whatever waits
at the bottom of all this altitude—
called *ordinary life*,
called *going on*,
called, simply,
*home*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness poem about leaving a version of yourself behind before an ascent, with vivid sensory and color imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Before the Climb**

I leave her folded in the grass like a coat too warm for this thin blue air—
her hands still smelling of woodsmoke and yesterday's bread,
her mouth full of all the words I meant to say and didn't.

Look how the mountain doesn't care.
Look how the granite goes on being gray and orange-veined
and older than any name I ever answered to.

I am walking out of my own shadow now,
the one that pooled black beneath the kitchen table,
black beneath the years of *not yet, not yet, not yet*—

and the sky is doing that thing at 5 a.m.
where it can't decide between violet and the color of a healing bruise,
and I think: yes. This is the hour for leaving things.

She will stay there in the low field, that other me,
picking at a hangnail of a life that fit too tight across the ribs,
counting clouds like sheep, like debts, like small mercies.

I take with me only the salt-taste of my own sweat,
the pine-green ache in my calves,
the way the wind up here smells like nothing—
like clean absence, like a page before the ink.

Somewhere below, she is already fading,
soft as a photograph left in a windowsill too long,
her cardigan the color of old rust, of *almost*, of *I couldn't*—

and I do not look back
because the trail is a silver thread unspooling
through granite the color of unspoken things,
and my lungs are burning gold with the going,

and there is a summit somewhere wearing the last of the night like a shawl,
and I am new the way a burn is new—
raw, and singing, and finally, finally light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free verse poem that explores grief through the metaphor of climbing a mountain, weaving in references to painting, dreams, and the body.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ascent

I did not choose this mountain. It rose
under my feet the night you stopped breathing,
and now I am always climbing,
lungs full of thin gray air,
hands raw from gripping what isn't there.

They say grief comes in stages
like base camps, like something you can prepare for
with the right gear, the right guide.
No one mentions the scree—
how each step forward slides you back,
how the body forgets how to want anything
but rest, but water, but the summit
that keeps rearranging itself
just out of reach.

In dreams I find you halfway up,
sitting on a rock the color of old bruises,
painting the valley below with colors
that don't exist in daylight—
cobalt where there should be green,
your brush moving like it used to move
before your hands forgot their language.
You never look up. You never see me
watching from the switchback,
afraid to call your name
in case the mountain swallows it,
in case you turn and I see
you've become the landscape.

My body has learned new grammars since you left.
The ache behind my sternum, permanent
as granite. The way my shoulders curl inward
like they're trying to become a cave,
someplace small enough to survive in.
Some mornings I wake with my jaw already clenched,
as if all night I'd been climbing too,
chasing you through switchbacks made of static,
through fog that tastes like the inside of your coat.

I keep a photograph of us at the trailhead—
before, when the mountain was just a mountain,
not yet this thing I live inside.
You're laughing at something out of frame.
I'm looking at you like you're the view.

Some days the air thins so much
I forget what I'm climbing toward.
I stop believing in summits.
I just move because the alternative
is staying still on this incline forever,
becoming another stone
you didn't see, didn't paint,
didn't need to remember.

But sometimes—rarely—
I reach a ridge where the wind clears
and I can see the whole shape of it:
this grief, this granite, this endless grade,
and somewhere in the valley below,
unreachable, ochre-colored,
still wet—

your last unfinished painting
of the two of us,
still climbing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective poem in long flowing lines about departure and self-fragmentation, using nature imagery (mist, snow, springs) and a recurring motif of a still-life painting.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Still Life Keeps**

I have been leaving myself in small increments, the way mist leaves a valley—
not all at once, but in slow surrenders, in threads unwinding from the greater cloud,
until what remains is only the shape of where fullness used to gather, a hollow
holding the memory of covering everything.

There is a painting I keep returning to in my mind: a pewter pitcher, three plums
going soft at their shoulders, a cloth draped over the table's edge like something
sleeping mid-fall, caught by the painter's hand before it could finish its collapse—
and I think this is what I am now, mid-collapse, held still by nothing
but the habit of appearing whole.

The snow does not ask permission to become water. It simply lets go
of its own architecture, the crystalline scaffolding it built all winter
to hold the shape of *snow*, and becomes instead a hundred small departures
running downhill, finding the path of least resistance, which is only
another way of saying *the path away from what I was.*

I keep packing boxes labeled with the wrong names. This one says *kitchen*
but holds instead the years I spent believing I was one continuous person,
not the plums going soft, not the pitcher tarnishing in its stillness,
not the cloth forever falling and never landing—
the painter's small mercy, to freeze me here, unbroken,
though I have already broken in every way that matters.

Somewhere the springs are opening in the hillside, water finding its way
up through stone that has held it prisoner all winter, and I think of how
the earth does not mourn what it releases—the springs simply arrive,
sudden and clear, as if they had never been anything else,
as if their long confinement was only a kind of waiting,
not an erasure.

I am trying to leave the way water leaves—not vanishing, only changing
containers, pouring myself from the shape I was into the shape
the leaving requires. But some nights I am only the still life again:
plums, pitcher, falling cloth, held in the museum-hush of what I used to be,
dust gathering on the frame while somewhere, underneath the paint,
something is still trying to finish its fall,
still trying to become the floor it was always reaching for,
still becoming, still becoming, though the picture insists
it has already arrived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
